entries.definition: A pathological condition that follows as a consequence of a disease, injury, or treatment.
entries.plain: A lasting after-effect of an illness or injury.
entries.etymology: Latin sequela 'that which follows', from sequi (to follow).
entries.exampleClinical: He recovered from the meningitis itself, but we're following him for neurological sequelae.
entries.exampleCasual: Honestly, my sleep schedule is a sequela of exam month — it never recovered.
entries.usageNote: Latin plural: sequelae /sɪˈkwɛliː/ — and the plural is what you'll say ninety percent of the time. Never 'sequelas'.

entries.definition: Developing so gradually that the disease is established before it produces obvious symptoms.
entries.plain: Creeping in slowly and quietly, without obvious warning.
entries.exampleClinical: Unlike the abrupt crush of an MI, her angina had an insidious onset over months of shrinking exercise tolerance.
entries.exampleCasual: Burnout is insidious — you don't notice it arriving until it's already moved in.
entries.usageNote: 'Insidious onset' is the fixed collocation in histories; its opposite in note-speak is 'abrupt' or 'acute onset'.

entries.definition: Occurring suddenly and with devastating severity and rapid progression.
entries.plain: Exploding into full force almost at once.
entries.etymology: Latin fulminare 'to strike with lightning', from fulmen (lightning bolt).
entries.exampleClinical: Within forty-eight hours the hepatitis declared itself fulminant, and we listed her for transplant.
entries.exampleCasual: His enthusiasm for the gym was fulminant — three sessions a day for a week, then nothing.
entries.usageNote: First syllable like 'full', not 'fyool'. Reserved for the most dramatic trajectories; don't dilute it on ordinary acute illness.

entries.definition: Of a disease: slow-growing, causing little pain, and progressing lazily over a long period.
entries.plain: Slow-moving and quiet, in no hurry to cause trouble.
entries.etymology: Latin indolens 'feeling no pain', from in- (not) + dolere (to feel pain).
entries.exampleClinical: The biopsy favored an indolent lymphoma, so the team chose surveillance over chemotherapy.
entries.exampleCasual: Outside the hospital, 'indolent' just means lazy — an indolent Sunday on the couch is excellent medicine.
entries.usageNote: A favorite in oncology. The everyday sense 'lazy' is literary; the clinical sense dominates in notes.

entries.definition: Protein-rich fluid that escapes from vessels into tissues or cavities due to increased vascular permeability, typically in inflammation.
entries.plain: Thick, protein-heavy fluid that leaks out of inflamed vessels.
entries.etymology: Latin exsudare 'to sweat out', from ex- (out) + sudare (to sweat).
entries.exampleClinical: Light's criteria called the effusion an exudate, which moved infection and malignancy to the top of the differential.
entries.exampleCasual: The wound was still producing exudate, so the dressing change was less fun than advertised.
entries.usageNote: Paired forever with 'transudate' — the protein-poor leak from pressure imbalance. The adjective is 'exudative'.

entries.definition: Protein-poor fluid pushed across intact vessel walls by hydrostatic or oncotic pressure imbalance rather than inflammation.
entries.plain: Watery fluid squeezed out of healthy vessels by pressure problems.
entries.exampleClinical: Bilateral effusions in a fluid-overloaded heart failure patient are almost always transudates — tap them only if something doesn't fit.
entries.exampleCasual: Exudate is the angry leak, transudate is the tired leak — that's how I kept them straight for the exam.
entries.usageNote: Stress the first syllable: TRAN-su-date. The exudate/transudate pair is a classic viva question, so own both words.

entries.definition: Characterized by the formation or discharge of pus.
entries.plain: Pus-forming.
entries.exampleClinical: The node went from reactive to frankly suppurative, and the fluctuance told us it was ready for drainage.
entries.exampleCasual: Medical English has a dozen elegant ways to say 'full of pus', and 'suppurative' is the dressiest.
entries.usageNote: Verb: to suppurate. Cousins: 'purulent' (made of pus) and 'pyogenic' (pus-generating) — all three live in the same paragraph of a textbook.

entries.definition: Of a disease: currently inactive or causing no symptoms, though not necessarily cured.
entries.plain: Quiet for now — asleep, not gone.
entries.exampleClinical: Her lupus has been quiescent on hydroxychloroquine for two years, so we're stretching the follow-up intervals.
entries.exampleCasual: My ambition to learn the guitar is quiescent — present, but showing no clinical activity.
entries.usageNote: Softer and more elegant than 'in remission'; common for chronic inflammatory disease (IBD, lupus, uveitis).

entries.definition: A sudden worsening or reactivation of a chronic disease.
entries.plain: A burst of disease activity after a quiet period.
entries.etymology: From the sense of a fire flaring up; origin uncertain.
entries.exampleClinical: She presented mid-flare: classic malar rash, joint pain, and a complement level scraping the floor.
entries.exampleCasual: Every conference deadline triggers a flare of my coffee dependence.
entries.usageNote: Noun and verb both work: 'the colitis flared'. 'Exacerbation' is the formal note word; 'flare' is what you say to patients and colleagues.

entries.definition: Of a sign or finding: so characteristic of a particular disease that it establishes the diagnosis by itself.
entries.plain: A finding that points to exactly one diagnosis.
entries.exampleClinical: Koplik spots are pathognomonic of measles — see them once and the workup is essentially over.
entries.exampleCasual: The silent group chat is pathognomonic of an exam tomorrow.
entries.usageNote: Pronounce the 'g': path-og-no-MON-ic. Takes 'of', never 'for'. Use sparingly — almost nothing truly is.

entries.definition: An early set of symptoms signalling that a disease is beginning, before the characteristic picture develops.
entries.plain: The warm-up symptoms before the main illness arrives.
entries.etymology: Greek prodromos 'running before', from pro- (before) + dromos (running).
entries.exampleClinical: He described a three-day viral prodrome — malaise, myalgia, low-grade temps — before the rash declared itself.
entries.exampleCasual: Yawning through the afternoon lecture is my migraine prodrome; I've learned to respect it.
entries.usageNote: Adjective: prodromal. A 'viral prodrome' is the stock phrase for the vague-flu opening act of many presentations.

entries.definition: A disturbance of normal physiological function or of laboratory values.
entries.plain: Something knocked out of its normal working order.
entries.etymology: French déranger 'to disturb', from des- (apart) + rang (rank, order).
entries.exampleClinical: The post-op labs showed a tidy collection of electrolyte derangements, none of them yet dangerous.
entries.exampleCasual: British colleagues say 'deranged LFTs' with a straight face, and it delights me every time.
entries.usageNote: In everyday English 'deranged' means insane — in medicine it just means 'abnormal'. Context does the work.

entries.definition: The passage of blood through the vascular bed of a tissue, delivering oxygen and nutrients.
entries.plain: How well blood is flowing through a tissue.
entries.etymology: Latin perfundere 'to pour over', from per- (through) + fundere (to pour).
entries.exampleClinical: Pressors brought the MAP up, but the mottled knees said end-organ perfusion was still lousy.
entries.exampleCasual: Don't confuse it with 'profusion' — an abundance. A profusion of bleeding is very bad for perfusion.
entries.usageNote: Verb: to perfuse. The bedside shorthand 'well-perfused' (warm, brisk capillary refill) appears in nearly every exam note.

entries.definition: Tissue death caused by interruption of its blood supply.
entries.plain: An area of tissue that died because its blood flow was cut off.
entries.etymology: Latin infarcire 'to stuff into' — early anatomists thought the dead tissue looked stuffed.
entries.exampleClinical: The lactate kept climbing despite fluids, and the CT confirmed what we feared: infarcted bowel.
entries.exampleCasual: The noun for the dead patch itself is 'infarct' — the process is 'infarction'. Examiners love that distinction.
entries.usageNote: Say in-FARK-shun. 'Infarct' (the lesion) vs 'infarction' (the event/process); the verb 'to infarct' exists and is common in speech.

entries.definition: Describing a physiological response that offsets the effect of a primary abnormality.
entries.plain: The body's counter-move to balance out a problem.
entries.exampleClinical: Her tachycardia was compensatory — treat the bleeding, not the heart rate.
entries.exampleCasual: Buying a fourth coffee is a compensatory mechanism for a decompensating sleep schedule.
entries.usageNote: The family matters: compensated → still coping; decompensated → coping failed. Learn the trio as one unit.

entries.definition: The failure of compensatory mechanisms, with clinical deterioration of a previously stable condition.
entries.plain: The moment the body's coping tricks stop working and the patient gets worse.
entries.exampleClinical: He's a compensated cirrhotic today, but one GI bleed could tip him into florid decompensation.
entries.exampleCasual: Saying 'the patient decompensated' sounds far more professional on rounds than 'he got worse fast'.
entries.usageNote: One of the highest-value verbs in ward English: 'to decompensate'. Pairs with cirrhosis, heart failure, and psychiatry alike.

entries.definition: Physical signs that collectively mark the presence of a particular disease.
entries.plain: The visible calling cards of a disease on the body.
entries.etymology: Greek stigma 'mark made by a pointed instrument, brand'.
entries.exampleClinical: Spider naevi, palmar erythema, gynecomastia — the stigmata of chronic liver disease were all on display.
entries.exampleCasual: Highlighters in four colors and an energy drink: the stigmata of finals week.
entries.usageNote: Already plural (singular 'stigma', rarely used clinically). The set phrase is 'stigmata of chronic liver disease' — say it as one breath.

entries.definition: Compression of the heart by fluid in the pericardial sac, impairing diastolic filling and cardiac output.
entries.plain: Fluid squeezing the heart from outside so it can't fill.
entries.exampleClinical: Beck's triad raised our suspicion for tamponade, so we rushed a bedside echo before the pressures bottomed out.
entries.exampleCasual: The board question described tamponade without ever using the word — muffled sounds, low BP, fat neck veins.
entries.usageNote: Stress the last syllable: tam-po-NADE. 'Tamponade physiology' describes the hemodynamics even before the full diagnosis.

entries.definition: Backward flow of blood through an incompetent valve; also the effortless return of gastric contents to the mouth.
entries.plain: Flow going backward through a leaky valve.
entries.etymology: Latin re- (back) + gurgitare (to flood), from gurges (whirlpool).
entries.exampleClinical: The echo graded the mitral regurgitation as moderate, with a posteriorly directed regurgitant jet.
entries.exampleCasual: Cardiologists say 'MR' and 'AR' so often you'd think the vowels were billed separately.
entries.usageNote: Adjective: regurgitant. A valve is 'incompetent' or 'leaky'; the opposite lesion is 'stenotic' (narrowed). Learn the pair.

entries.definition: Abnormal narrowing of a valve, vessel, or other tubular structure.
entries.plain: A passage that has become too narrow.
entries.exampleClinical: Syncope on exertion in an elderly man with a crescendo-decrescendo murmur — assume critical aortic stenosis until the echo says otherwise.
entries.exampleCasual: Plural is 'stenoses', which always sounds like a Greek island to me.
entries.usageNote: Adjective: stenotic; verb in reports: 'stenosed'. Plural: stenoses /stɛˈnoʊsiːz/.

entries.definition: An abnormal whooshing sound heard over a vessel, produced by turbulent blood flow.
entries.plain: A whoosh you hear with the stethoscope over a narrowed artery.
entries.exampleClinical: Before clearing him for surgery, listen over both carotids — a bruit there changes the conversation.
entries.exampleCasual: The pronunciation trap of the cardiology rotation: 'broo-EE', the French way, not 'broot'.
entries.usageNote: Most American clinicians say /ˈbruːi/ — the final 't' stays silent either way. A bruit is vascular; a 'murmur' is cardiac.

entries.definition: Cramping limb pain induced by exertion and relieved by rest, caused by inadequate arterial supply.
entries.plain: Leg pain that comes on with walking and fades with rest, from clogged arteries.
entries.etymology: Latin claudicare 'to limp', from claudus (lame) — Emperor Claudius limped.
entries.exampleClinical: His claudication distance has shrunk from four blocks to one, which is the disease telling us its pace.
entries.exampleCasual: 'Claudication distance' — how far you walk before the pain stops you — is one of those terms that's secretly just a number.
entries.usageNote: Distinguish vascular claudication (relieved by standing still) from neurogenic 'pseudoclaudication' of spinal stenosis (relieved by bending forward).

entries.definition: Breathlessness that appears when lying flat and is relieved by sitting or standing.
entries.plain: Needing to sit up to breathe comfortably.
entries.exampleClinical: She sleeps on three pillows now — quantify the orthopnea and you've quantified the failure.
entries.exampleCasual: History-taking pro move: ask 'how many pillows?' instead of 'do you get breathless lying down?'.
entries.usageNote: Travels with PND (paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea) in every heart-failure history. Counted in pillows by ancient convention.

entries.definition: Occurring in sudden, recurrent episodes that start and stop abruptly.
entries.plain: Coming in sudden attacks, out of nowhere.
entries.etymology: Greek paroxysmos 'irritation, sharpening', from para- (beyond) + oxynein (to sharpen).
entries.exampleClinical: Her palpitations are paroxysmal — racing for an hour, then gone — so we sent her home with an event monitor.
entries.exampleCasual: The noun is lovely too: 'paroxysms of laughter' is the official diagnosis of our study group at 2 a.m.
entries.usageNote: In AF classification, 'paroxysmal' means self-terminating within seven days — it's a defined term, not just a flavor word.

entries.definition: Sweating profusely, especially as a sign of physiological distress.
entries.plain: Drenched in sweat.
entries.etymology: Greek diaphorein 'to carry through, disperse (by sweat)'.
entries.exampleClinical: He arrived clutching his chest, pale and diaphoretic — the kind of sweat you can see from the doorway.
entries.exampleCasual: 'Pale and diaphoretic' is ER shorthand for 'this one is actually sick'.
entries.usageNote: Noun: diaphoresis. 'Pale and diaphoretic' functions as a single fixed phrase signalling genuine illness.

entries.definition: Of a pulse: barely perceptible, weak, and fine like a thread.
entries.plain: A pulse so weak it feels like a thin thread under the finger.
entries.exampleClinical: Pulse rapid and thready, skin cool and clammy — shock until proven otherwise.
entries.exampleCasual: The opposite is a 'bounding' pulse — the artery practically introduces itself.
entries.usageNote: 'Rapid and thready' vs 'full and bounding' are the two stock pulse descriptions; everything else is commentary.

entries.definition: To listen to internal body sounds, typically with a stethoscope, as part of examination.
entries.plain: To listen to the body with a stethoscope.
entries.exampleClinical: Auscultate the bases before you read the chest film — the crackles will tell you where to look.
entries.exampleCasual: Verbs of the physical exam: inspect, palpate, percuss, auscultate — in that ceremonial order.
entries.usageNote: The noun phrase 'on auscultation' opens half the chest findings ever written. Don't write 'auscultated clear' — 'clear to auscultation' is the idiom.

entries.definition: Discontinuous popping sounds heard over the lungs, produced by the reopening of collapsed or fluid-filled small airways.
entries.plain: Popping lung sounds, like Velcro or fizzing bubbles.
entries.etymology: Imitative; the older synonym 'rales' is from French râle (rattle).
entries.exampleClinical: Fine, Velcro-like crackles at both bases — in a chronically breathless patient, think fibrosis before failure.
entries.exampleCasual: Americans say crackles, the British say crepitations, the old guard says rales; the lungs don't care.
entries.usageNote: 'Bibasilar crackles' is the heart-failure cliché. Fine vs coarse, inspiratory timing, and whether they clear with cough all carry meaning.

entries.definition: A continuous, musical, high-pitched sound from narrowed lower airways, usually expiratory.
entries.plain: A musical whistling sound from tight airways.
entries.exampleClinical: Diffuse polyphonic wheeze with a silent right base — never let the loud sounds distract you from the quiet zone.
entries.exampleCasual: Wheeze is the airway's whistle; stridor is its scream — one is a clinic visit, the other is a crash call.
entries.usageNote: Wheeze = lower airways, mostly expiratory. Stridor = upper airway, mostly inspiratory, and an emergency word. Never swap them.

entries.definition: A harsh, high-pitched inspiratory sound caused by turbulent flow through an obstructed upper airway.
entries.plain: A harsh crowing sound when breathing in — the upper airway is blocking.
entries.exampleClinical: Drooling, tripod position, inspiratory stridor — nobody examines that throat until the airway team is in the room.
entries.exampleCasual: If a question mentions stridor, the answer involves securing the airway; everything else is decoration.
entries.usageNote: An alarm-bell word: say it and people move faster. 'Stridor at rest' marks severity in croup grading.

entries.definition: Coughing up blood originating from the airways or lungs.
entries.plain: Coughing up blood.
entries.exampleClinical: Weight loss, night sweats, and a month of hemoptysis in a smoker — the bronchoscopy books itself.
entries.exampleCasual: Hemoptysis comes from the lungs, hematemesis from the gut; mixing them up sends the workup in the wrong direction entirely.
entries.usageNote: Stress: he-MOP-ti-sis. 'Massive hemoptysis' is defined by volume and threat to the airway, not drama.

entries.definition: Mucus and other material coughed up from the lower airways, examined for color, volume, and content.
entries.plain: What you cough up from the chest.
entries.exampleClinical: Frothy pink sputum in a hypertensive crisis is pulmonary edema announcing itself.
entries.exampleCasual: Half of pulmonology is asking polite, detailed questions about sputum and keeping a straight face.
entries.usageNote: The verb 'to expectorate' (to cough up) is the formal cousin of 'to bring up'. Descriptors do the diagnostic work: purulent, rusty, frothy, blood-tinged.

entries.definition: Collapse or incomplete expansion of lung tissue with loss of volume.
entries.plain: Part of the lung has deflated like a flat sponge.
entries.exampleClinical: Post-op day one fever with basal atelectasis: get her sitting up, breathing deep, and using the incentive spirometer.
entries.exampleCasual: At-uh-LEK-tuh-sis — five syllables that flunk more pronunciation tests than any other chest word.
entries.usageNote: Stress the 'lek': a-te-LEC-ta-sis. Adjective: atelectatic. Radiology reports love 'subsegmental atelectasis' for small streaks.

entries.definition: To place a tube into the trachea to secure the airway and enable mechanical ventilation.
entries.plain: To put a breathing tube down the windpipe.
entries.exampleClinical: His gases were drifting the wrong way all night; by dawn the question wasn't whether to intubate but who would.
entries.exampleCasual: The airway verbs come as a set: intubate, extubate, and — the gentle middle path — 'trial of extubation'.
entries.usageNote: Family: extubate (remove the tube), reintubate (the verb nobody wants). 'Tubed' is common spoken shorthand.

entries.definition: To withdraw a patient gradually from a therapy on which they have become dependent, such as a ventilator or a drug.
entries.plain: To slowly reduce support until it can be stopped.
entries.etymology: Old English wenian 'to accustom' — originally of infants and breastfeeding.
entries.exampleClinical: We'll wean the pressors overnight and see whether his own vasculature is ready to take the job back.
entries.exampleCasual: I'm weaning myself off checking my phone during lectures, with about the same success rate as a difficult vent wean.
entries.usageNote: Takes 'off': wean off the vent, off steroids. As a noun: 'a slow steroid wean'. 'Taper' overlaps but is drug-specific.

entries.definition: Elevation of nitrogenous waste products (urea, creatinine) in the blood, usually from reduced renal clearance.
entries.plain: Waste chemicals building up in the blood because the kidneys aren't clearing them.
entries.etymology: French azote 'nitrogen' (Greek a- + zoe, 'without life') + -emia (blood condition).
entries.exampleClinical: Dry mucous membranes, a BUN-to-creatinine ratio over twenty — classic prerenal azotemia begging for fluid.
entries.exampleCasual: Azotemia is the number on the lab sheet; uremia is when the patient starts feeling that number.
entries.usageNote: Key contrast: azotemia = biochemical; uremia = symptomatic azotemia (nausea, pruritus, pericardial rub). The trio prerenal/intrinsic/postrenal organizes the workup.

entries.definition: Producing abnormally small volumes of urine, conventionally under about 400 mL per day in adults.
entries.plain: Making too little urine.
entries.exampleClinical: She's been oliguric since midnight despite two liters of crystalloid — time to look beyond the prerenal story.
entries.exampleCasual: The urine-output ladder: polyuric, normal, oliguric, anuric — a whole vocabulary for one catheter bag.
entries.usageNote: Family: oliguria (noun), anuria (essentially none), polyuria (too much). Hourly output 'mL/kg/hr' is how the ICU actually talks about it.

entries.definition: To treat a patient with dialysis, clearing solutes and fluid that failing kidneys cannot remove.
entries.plain: To run a patient's blood through a filtering machine.
entries.etymology: Greek dialysis 'a loosening apart', from dia- (through) + lyein (to loosen).
entries.exampleClinical: Refractory hyperkalemia with ECG changes — stop optimizing and dialyze him tonight.
entries.exampleCasual: The mnemonic AEIOU lists the reasons to dialyze emergently; remembering it is easier than spelling 'hyperkalemia' at 3 a.m.
entries.usageNote: 'Dialysis-dependent' marks chronicity in one word. Spoken wards shorten everything: 'He's an HD patient, runs Tuesday-Thursday-Saturday.'

entries.definition: To urinate; the standard clinical verb for emptying the bladder.
entries.plain: To pee, in polite chart language.
entries.exampleClinical: He hasn't voided since the spinal wore off — scan the bladder before it scans you.
entries.exampleCasual: Chart English is its own dialect: patients pee, but in the note they 'void without difficulty'.
entries.usageNote: 'Post-void residual' (PVR) is the bladder-scan number everyone asks for. History-taking trio: urgency, frequency, hesitancy.

entries.definition: Of pain: coming in waves of cramping that build, peak, and ease, typical of obstruction of a hollow organ.
entries.plain: Cramping pain that comes and goes in waves.
entries.exampleClinical: Loin-to-groin colicky pain with a patient who can't lie still — renal colic until the CT says otherwise.
entries.exampleCasual: Peritonitis patients lie statue-still; colic patients writhe — you can almost diagnose from the doorway choreography.
entries.usageNote: Colicky pain = hollow-organ obstruction (ureter, gut, biliary tree). The patient who cannot get comfortable is the textbook picture.

entries.definition: Reflex or voluntary contraction of abdominal wall muscles on palpation, protecting inflamed structures beneath.
entries.plain: Belly muscles tensing up to protect something sore inside.
entries.etymology: From 'guard' — the muscles literally stand guard.
entries.exampleClinical: There's involuntary guarding in the right lower quadrant with rebound — book the appendix before it books itself.
entries.exampleCasual: Voluntary guarding means the patient is nervous; involuntary guarding means the peritoneum is.
entries.usageNote: The crescendo of peritoneal signs: tenderness → guarding → rigidity. 'Involuntary' is the word that escalates the phone call.

entries.definition: Board-like involuntary stiffness of the abdominal wall indicating generalized peritonitis; in neurology, increased muscle tone throughout movement.
entries.plain: A belly gone hard as a board because the lining inside is inflamed everywhere.
entries.exampleClinical: A silent, board-like abdomen two days after a missed perforation — rigidity is the exam finding nobody argues with.
entries.exampleCasual: Same word, two worlds: surgeons hear 'rigidity' and think laparotomy; neurologists think Parkinson's cogwheel.
entries.usageNote: Abdominal rigidity = surgical emergency register. Neurological rigidity (cogwheel, lead-pipe) is a different exam and a different floor.

entries.definition: Black, tarry, foul-smelling stool produced by digested blood from an upper gastrointestinal source.
entries.plain: Black tar-like stool from blood that's been digested on the way down.
entries.exampleClinical: Two days of melena and a hemoglobin down three points — the bleed is upper until endoscopy proves otherwise.
entries.exampleCasual: Melena means it's been digested (upper source); hematochezia is fresh red (usually lower) — geography by color.
entries.usageNote: Adjective: melenic. Iron and bismuth also blacken stool — 'true melena' has the unmistakable tarry sheen and smell.

entries.definition: Passage of fresh, bright-red blood per rectum, usually from a lower gastrointestinal source.
entries.plain: Bright red blood in the stool.
entries.exampleClinical: Brisk hematochezia can still be an upper bleed moving fast — if he's unstable, scope from the top first.
entries.exampleCasual: The ward writes it as BRBPR — bright red blood per rectum — because nobody trusts their spelling of hematochezia on night shift.
entries.usageNote: Spoken alternative: 'BRBPR', said letter by letter. The melena/hematochezia pair locates the bleed; learn them together.

entries.definition: Showing jaundice — yellow discoloration of skin or sclerae from elevated bilirubin.
entries.plain: Yellow-tinged, from bilirubin building up.
entries.exampleClinical: Check the sclerae in daylight — scleral icterus shows itself long before the skin admits anything.
entries.exampleCasual: 'Anicteric' earns its keep in notes: one word for 'not yellow, I did look'.
entries.usageNote: Noun: icterus. Sclerae show it first (around bilirubin 2–3 mg/dL). 'Jaundiced' is what you tell the patient; 'icteric' is what you write.

entries.definition: A persistent, painful sensation of needing to defecate despite an empty rectum.
entries.plain: Feeling you urgently need to go even though nothing is there.
entries.etymology: Greek teinesmos, from teinein (to stretch, strain).
entries.exampleClinical: Bloody diarrhea with tenesmus localizes the colitis distally — the rectum is where that symptom lives.
entries.exampleCasual: Tenesmus is one of those words patients describe perfectly without ever knowing it has a name.
entries.usageNote: Strongly associated with proctitis and rectal involvement in IBD. There is also vesical tenesmus, the urinary cousin.

entries.definition: Audible rumbling or gurgling sounds produced by movement of gas and fluid through the intestines.
entries.plain: Loud stomach rumbling.
entries.etymology: Greek borborygmos, an onomatopoeia for gut gurgling.
entries.exampleClinical: High-pitched, tinkling borborygmi against a backdrop of colicky pain — early obstruction has a soundtrack.
entries.exampleCasual: Borborygmi: the official medical spelling of the noise your stomach makes in a quiet exam hall.
entries.usageNote: Already plural (singular: borborygmus). One of the few onomatopoeic words in medicine — say it aloud and you'll hear why.

entries.definition: Therapeutic or diagnostic washing-out of a body cavity or organ with fluid.
entries.plain: Rinsing out a body space with fluid.
entries.etymology: French laver 'to wash', from Latin lavare.
entries.exampleClinical: The pneumonia wasn't growing anything, so pulmonology went in for a bronchoalveolar lavage to interrogate it properly.
entries.exampleCasual: Keep the French pronunciation — luh-VAHZH — and you'll sound like you've actually done one.
entries.usageNote: BAL (bronchoalveolar lavage) is said as letters. Verb use exists: 'the joint was lavaged in theatre'.

entries.definition: Diversion of blood along an abnormal or alternative path, bypassing normal circulation or ventilation.
entries.plain: Blood taking a detour around where it should go.
entries.etymology: From railway 'shunt' — to divert onto another track.
entries.exampleClinical: His hypoxia barely budged on 100% oxygen — that refractoriness is the signature of true shunting.
entries.exampleCasual: Physiology in one line: dead space is ventilation without perfusion; shunt is perfusion without ventilation.
entries.usageNote: Both noun and verb ('blood shunts right-to-left'). Also a device: a VP shunt drains CSF — same word, different gadget.

entries.definition: A triple cadence of heart sounds produced by an audible third or fourth heart sound, resembling a horse's gallop.
entries.plain: An extra heart sound that makes the rhythm sound like galloping hooves.
entries.etymology: From the rhythm's resemblance to a galloping horse.
entries.exampleClinical: A new S3 gallop in a breathless thirty-year-old reframes everything — young hearts shouldn't gallop.
entries.exampleCasual: S3 sounds like 'Ken-tuck-y', S4 like 'Ten-nes-see' — American states, donated to cardiology forever.
entries.usageNote: An S3 can be normal in the young and athletic; in the breathless adult it means volume overload. 'Gallop' alone usually implies S3.

entries.definition: A palpable vibration over the precordium or a vessel, produced by turbulent flow — a murmur you can feel.
entries.plain: A buzzing vibration you can feel with your hand over the heart.
entries.exampleClinical: If you can feel a thrill, the murmur is grade four or louder by definition — grading made tactile.
entries.exampleCasual: A fistula that works has a thrill; the dialysis nurses check it like clockwork.
entries.usageNote: Murmur = heard; thrill = felt. A thrill over a dialysis fistula is reassurance, not pathology.

entries.definition: Showing bluish discoloration of skin or mucous membranes from inadequate oxygenation of blood.
entries.plain: Turned blue from too little oxygen.
entries.exampleClinical: Check the tongue: central cyanosis lives there, while cold blue fingertips may just be a cold room.
entries.exampleCasual: 'Dusky' is the gentler bedside word that nurses use before anyone says 'cyanotic' out loud.
entries.usageNote: Central (tongue, lips — true hypoxemia) vs peripheral (fingertips — sluggish flow). Noun: cyanosis.

entries.definition: Showing a patchy, lace-like discoloration of the skin from uneven perfusion, often a sign of shock.
entries.plain: Skin with a blotchy purple net pattern from poor blood flow.
entries.exampleClinical: The blood pressure looked respectable, but the mottling creeping past her knees disagreed with it.
entries.exampleCasual: ICU wisdom: trust the knees — mottling there often outruns the monitor.
entries.usageNote: Mottling over the knees is so prognostic in septic shock that there's a formal 'mottling score'. Verb: to mottle.

entries.definition: Transient loss of consciousness from global cerebral hypoperfusion, with spontaneous complete recovery.
entries.plain: Fainting — a brief blackout from the brain not getting enough blood.
entries.etymology: Greek synkope 'a cutting short', from syn- (together) + koptein (to cut).
entries.exampleClinical: Syncope on exertion is a structural-heart red flag; syncope at the sight of blood usually just needs a chair.
entries.exampleCasual: Three syllables, not two: SIN-ko-pee. Mispronounce it and the attending will faint.
entries.usageNote: Adjective: syncopal; the warning state is 'presyncope'. Patients say 'passed out' — translate both directions fluently.

entries.definition: An unpleasant subjective awareness of one's own heartbeat — racing, pounding, fluttering, or skipping.
entries.plain: Feeling your own heartbeat in an uncomfortable way.
entries.etymology: Latin palpitare 'to throb', frequentative of palpare (to touch gently).
entries.exampleClinical: Ask her to tap the rhythm on the desk — a tapped-out irregularly irregular beat is half an ECG already.
entries.exampleCasual: Palpitations are what the patient feels; palpation is what your hands do — one letter, two different exams.
entries.usageNote: Nearly always plural. The palpation/palpitation mix-up is the classic learner's slip — see the Mix-ups tab.

entries.definition: To induce increased urine output, typically with diuretics, in order to remove excess fluid.
entries.plain: To make a patient pee off extra fluid with medication.
entries.etymology: Back-formation from diuresis; Greek dia- (through) + ouresis (urination).
entries.exampleClinical: He's three liters up since admission — diurese him gently overnight and reassess the creatinine at dawn.
entries.exampleCasual: 'Diurese to euvolemia' is the cardiology haiku: remove water until the body is balanced.
entries.usageNote: Ward verb par excellence; the noun is diuresis, the drugs are diuretics, the goal is 'euvolemia'. 'Brisk diuresis' = it's working.

entries.definition: Heartbeats arising from sites other than the sinus node; more generally, tissue located where it doesn't belong.
entries.plain: Extra beats firing from the wrong part of the heart.
entries.exampleClinical: Telemetry showed runs of ventricular ectopy overnight — check the potassium and magnesium before anything fancier.
entries.exampleCasual: The same root gives 'ectopic pregnancy' — out-of-place is a whole theme in medicine.
entries.usageNote: On the wards, 'ectopy' almost always means extra beats on the monitor. Adjective: ectopic; a single beat is 'an ectopic'.

entries.definition: Shallow, restricted breathing adopted to avoid pain from chest-wall or pleural irritation; also immobilizing a limb with a splint.
entries.plain: Breathing shallowly on purpose because deep breaths hurt.
entries.etymology: From 'splint' — the patient stiffens the painful area as if bracing it.
entries.exampleClinical: She's splinting from the rib fractures, which is exactly how an atelectasis and a pneumonia get invited in.
entries.exampleCasual: Post-op patients splint when they laugh — hence the pillow hugged to every abdominal incision.
entries.usageNote: Pain control isn't a luxury here: splinting → hypoventilation → atelectasis → pneumonia is a chain worth reciting.

entries.definition: Of chest pain: sharp and worsened by inspiration, coughing, or movement of the pleura.
entries.plain: Chest pain that stabs when you breathe in.
entries.exampleClinical: Sudden pleuritic pain with a swollen calf — that sentence is a CT pulmonary angiogram in disguise.
entries.exampleCasual: Describing pain in one adjective — pleuritic, colicky, crushing — is the fastest way to sound fluent on rounds.
entries.usageNote: 'Pleuritic' answers the quality question for chest pain; its archetypes are PE, pneumothorax, and pericarditis (worse lying flat).

entries.definition: Replacement of alveolar air by fluid, pus, or cells, making lung tissue dense — the radiological and exam signature of pneumonia.
entries.plain: A patch of lung filled with fluid or pus instead of air.
entries.exampleClinical: Dullness, bronchial breathing, and crackles over the right base — the exam called the consolidation before the film did.
entries.exampleCasual: Radiology hedges with 'airspace opacity'; clinicians translate that to consolidation and start antibiotics.
entries.usageNote: Exam triad over consolidation: dull percussion, bronchial breath sounds, increased vocal resonance. The verb 'consolidate' appears in reports.

entries.definition: Having an abnormally high arterial carbon dioxide level, usually from ventilatory failure.
entries.plain: Too much carbon dioxide in the blood because breathing can't blow it off.
entries.exampleClinical: Drowsy with a flapping tremor and a gas full of CO2 — hypercapnic failure, and the BiPAP mask is the next sentence.
entries.exampleCasual: Type 1 failure: oxygen problem. Type 2: oxygen plus CO2 problem. 'Hypercapnic' is the word that flags type 2.
entries.usageNote: Noun: hypercapnia. The spoken ward synonym is 'a CO2 retainer'. The flapping tremor is 'asterixis' — another word worth owning.

entries.definition: Displacement of the trachea from the midline, indicating a pressure or volume imbalance between the two hemithoraces.
entries.plain: The windpipe pushed off to one side.
entries.etymology: Trachea from Greek tracheia (rough artery); deviation from Latin deviare (to turn from the road).
collocations: tracheal deviation away from the affected side
entries.exampleClinical: Hypotension, a silent hyperresonant left chest, and tracheal deviation to the right — needle first, image later.
entries.exampleCasual: Exam logic: tension pushes the trachea away; collapse pulls it toward — one preposition decides the diagnosis.
entries.usageNote: Notes record the normal as 'trachea central'. 'Deviated away' = pushing lesion (tension pneumothorax, effusion); 'toward' = pulling lesion (collapse).

entries.definition: Foamy or bubbly; of urine, suggesting heavy proteinuria; of sputum, suggesting pulmonary edema.
entries.plain: Foamy, like beaten egg whites.
entries.exampleClinical: He mentioned, almost in passing, that his urine had turned frothy — and the dipstick promptly explained why.
entries.exampleCasual: A barista word doing serious nephrology work: frothy urine is protein until proven otherwise.
entries.usageNote: Two organs, one adjective: frothy urine → nephrotic-range proteinuria; frothy pink sputum → pulmonary edema. Context picks the emergency.

entries.definition: Hidden from direct observation; detectable only by testing.
entries.plain: Present but invisible — only a test can find it.
entries.etymology: Latin occultus 'hidden', from occulere (to cover up).
entries.exampleClinical: Iron deficiency in a sixty-year-old man is occult GI blood loss until colonoscopy says otherwise.
entries.exampleCasual: Nothing supernatural — in medicine 'occult' just means hiding from the naked eye.
entries.usageNote: The antonym in clinical English is 'frank' or 'overt': occult blood vs frank blood. FOBT = fecal occult blood test.

entries.definition: Unmistakable and fully evident; clinically obvious to direct observation.
entries.plain: Plain to see — no test needed.
entries.etymology: From 'frank' meaning open, candid — Old French franc (free).
entries.exampleClinical: What began as guaiac-positive stool by morning had become frank melena, and the urgency changed with the adjective.
entries.exampleCasual: Medical 'frank' has nothing to do with honesty — frank pus is simply pus you can see.
entries.usageNote: Adverb form is common too: 'frankly purulent', 'frankly icteric'. Its mirror-twin 'occult' completes the pair.

entries.definition: Fully developed and dramatic in presentation; showing the complete, exuberant picture of a disease.
entries.plain: The disease in full bloom, with every feature on display.
entries.exampleClinical: By the time she reached us the myxedema was florid — the textbook page had stood up and walked in.
entries.exampleCasual: Also said of prose: a florid essay is one drowning in adjectives, which is a kind of pathology too.
entries.usageNote: Implies dramatic completeness, often with a hint that it should have been caught earlier. 'Full-blown' is the plainer synonym.

entries.definition: To cough up and spit out material from the airways.
entries.plain: To cough something up and spit it out.
entries.etymology: Latin expectorare 'to drive from the chest', from ex- (out) + pectus (chest).
entries.exampleClinical: She's too weak to expectorate effectively, so the secretions pool and the chest physio earns their keep.
entries.exampleCasual: Patients 'bring up phlegm'; charts say 'expectorate' — same act, different dress code.
entries.usageNote: Literally 'out of the chest' — a perfect morpheme specimen. An 'expectorant' is a drug meant to help it along.

entries.definition: Difficulty initiating urination despite the urge to void, typical of bladder outlet obstruction.
entries.plain: Standing there ready to go, but the stream won't start.
entries.exampleClinical: Hesitancy, a weak stream, and nocturia three times nightly — the prostate is writing this history.
entries.exampleCasual: The urinary history is a fixed playlist: urgency, frequency, hesitancy, nocturia, dribbling — learn it as a song.
entries.usageNote: One of the 'LUTS' (lower urinary tract symptoms) — an abbreviation said as a word, 'luts'. General sense 'reluctance' also exists; context separates them.

entries.definition: Swelling or enlargement of a structure or cavity from internal pressure, such as gas, fluid, or blood.
entries.plain: Swollen and stretched from the inside.
entries.etymology: Latin distendere 'to stretch apart', from dis- (apart) + tendere (to stretch).
entries.exampleClinical: The abdomen was tympanitic and visibly distended, with the old scars hinting at the adhesions underneath.
entries.exampleCasual: Patients say bloated; the note says distended; the surgeon says 'how distended, exactly?'.
entries.usageNote: Both 'distension' and 'distention' are correct spellings; pick one and be consistent. JVD = jugular venous distension.

entries.definition: The internal environment or setting in which physiological processes occur.
entries.plain: The internal environment surrounding cells and processes.
entries.etymology: French milieu 'middle place', from mi (mid) + lieu (place).
entries.exampleClinical: Correct the metabolic milieu first — potassium, magnesium, pH — or the arrhythmia will simply reload.
entries.exampleCasual: Claude Bernard's 'milieu intérieur' is the ancestor of everything we mean by homeostasis.
entries.usageNote: French plural 'milieux'. In psychiatry, 'milieu therapy' means the treatment environment itself — same word, different ward.

entries.definition: The isolation or pooling of blood, fluid, or tissue away from effective circulation or normal connection.
entries.plain: A portion of blood or tissue trapped where the body can't use it.
entries.etymology: Latin sequestrare 'to set aside, deposit in safekeeping'.
entries.exampleClinical: In pancreatitis, liters can vanish into third-space sequestration while the blood pressure quietly follows.
entries.exampleCasual: The same word describes a kid's spleen hoarding platelets and a senator's frozen budget — sequestration is universal.
entries.usageNote: 'Third-spacing' is the spoken verb form of the fluid sense. A 'sequestrum' is dead bone walled off in osteomyelitis — same root.
